newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S., Mexico sign money laundering, other accords.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico sign money laundering, other accords.

text.p: The United States and Mexico hope to crack down on rampant laundering of drug money in Mexico under an agreement signed to mark U.S. President Bill Clinton's first official visit to Mexico.
The agreement was one of a clutch of accords signed by a Bi-National Commission grouping cabinet officials of both countries and presented on Tuesday to Clinton and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo.
Others covered subjects ranging from law enforcement cooperation along the two countries' 2,000-mile (3,200-km) common border to the environment, civil aviation and culture.
At the presentation ceremony, Clinton stressed the aim of overcoming a legacy of border problems dating from 19th century wars to drug trafficking and illegal migration today.

"In the 21st century, we want our border to be our bond, and we want it to be rooted in a mutual commitment to the exchange of people and commerce across the border and to our fidelity to the rule of law," he said.

Drug money laundering has become a serious problem in Mexico, where the government only made it a crime last year and only recently issued regulations to financial institutions to allow better tracing of illegal assets.

Officials said this week's agreement, which was in addition to a joint declaration on anti-drug efforts signed on Tuesday, would improve exchange of information on currency transactions between the two countries to better track money laundering.
Full details of the accord were not immediately available, but a senior U.S. official said it involved swapping information "basically on transactions that involve large amounts of cash".
The United States will provide computers and training to Mexico's Secretariat of Finance to help it investigate and prosecute money laundering.
Other agreements signed by the commission, holding its 14th annual session, included:

-- a cost-sharing agreement to operate a waste-water plant near San Diego, California, to treat raw sewage flowing into the United States from the Tijuana region of Mexico; the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will grant $170 million to the North American Development Bank to fund water projects in border regions;

-- exchanges of documents to mark beginning of construction of a third bridge across the Rio Grande between Brownsville, Texas, and Matamoros, Mexico, and approving reopening of an improved existing bridge;
-- an exchange of documents to expand a liaison mechanism to handle law enforcement along the border;
-- an exchange of documents specifying radio frequencies used by emergency services in fire-fighting and other operations along the border;
-- a letter of intent on two agreements covering civil aviation technical assistance and cooperation in development of aviation technology;
-- amendment of a 1936 treaty on migratory birds to allow native communities in parts of Alaska to harvest waterfowl;
-- a letter of intent to increase scientific and technical exchanges on parklands and protected areas along the border, and strengthen land management and monitoring activities;
-- a memorandum of understanding to integrate the two countries' programmes on forest, soil and water issues;
-- an exchange of documents to expand the U.S. Fulbright programme for Mexican graduate students of science and technology including free transportation by selected American and Mexican air carriers.
